name: South Korea
traditionNote: A codified civil-law system on a German-Japanese model: the binding rule is the enacted statutory text, not the judgment, so research starts at the consolidated code on law.go.kr and only then moves to Supreme Court and Constitutional Court decisions for interpretation.
summary: Acts (법률) are passed by the unicameral National Assembly and promulgated by the President; the executive issues Presidential Decrees (대통령령), Prime Minister's and Ministerial Ordinances (총리령·부령), and administrative rules beneath them. Promulgation happens by publication in the Gwanbo, the official gazette, now published electronically at gwanbo.go.kr by the Ministry of the Interior and Safety. Under Article 53 of the Constitution an Act takes effect twenty days after promulgation unless the Act itself sets a different enforcement date, and most do. The authentic text is the Korean text as promulgated in the gazette; the consolidated, currently-in-force version maintained by the Ministry of Government Legislation at the National Law Information Center (law.go.kr) is the working text everyone actually uses. Every English version of a Korean statute, including the Constitution, is an unofficial reference translation with no legal effect.
hierarchy: Treaties duly concluded and promulgated, and generally recognised rules of international law (same effect as domestic Acts)
Prime Minister's Ordinances and Ministerial Ordinances / Enforcement Rules (총리령·부령·시행규칙)
Local ordinances (조례) and local government rules (규칙)

gazette.name: Daehanmingug Jeonja Gwanbo
gazette.en: Electronic Official Gazette of the Republic of Korea
gazette.authority: Ministry of the Interior and Safety (행정안전부)
gazette.coverage: September 1948-present; the site reports over 546,000 gazette documents. Post-2001 fully searchable online; 1948-2000 paper gazettes digitised by the National Archives and searchable through the advanced-search screen. Agency/department/legal-basis metadata search only works for gazettes from 25 March 2021 onward.
gazette.desc: The gazette of record. An Act, decree, treaty or ministerial ordinance is legally promulgated by being published here, so this is where the authentic as-promulgated text lives, along with public notices, legislative announcements, civil-servant asset disclosures and naturalisation lists.
gazette.howto: Use 기본검색 for anything after 2001: enter the instrument name or keyword and choose whether to match 제목 (title only) or 제목+본문 (title and full text). To jump straight to an issue use 호수별 (by issue number), 일자별 (by date) or 기간별 (by date range). For a pre-2001 promulgation switch to 고급검색 and use the separate pre-2001 archive block, filtering by 편집구분 (e.g. 법률, 대통령령) and date range.
gazette.note: The gazette gives you the text as promulgated on that day only; it never shows the current consolidated version of a law. For that, go to law.go.kr.

constitution.name: Daehanmingug Heonbeop
constitution.en: Constitution of the Republic of Korea
constitution.coverage: Ninth amendment: 헌법 제10호, wholly revised 29 October 1987, in force from 25 February 1988. Earlier constitutions from 1948 onward are available as historical versions (연혁).
constitution.desc: The official current text of the 1987 Constitution on the National Law Information Center, carrying the promulgation number and enforcement date and linked to the implementing Acts, Constitutional Court decisions and historical versions.
constitution.howto: Open the 본문 (body) tab for the running text by chapter and article; 연혁 lists all nine prior constitutional texts back to 1948; 3단비교 shows an article next to its implementing statutes and decrees.
constitution.note: Only the Korean text is authentic. The English version at law.go.kr/LSW/eng/engLsInfoR.do?lsiSeq=61603 carries an explicit disclaimer that it has no legal authority or official effect.

sources.name: Gukga Beomnyeong Jeongbo Center
sources.coverage: All Acts, Presidential Decrees and ministerial ordinances currently in force, plus historical (연혁) versions, administrative rules, local ordinances, treaties, court and Constitutional Court decisions, and ministry legal interpretations.
sources.desc: The single most important legal site in Korea and the government's official consolidated database. It is where you get the currently-in-force text of any statute with its amendment history, its enforcement decree and enforcement rule side by side, and links to the cases and interpretations applying it.
sources.howto: Type the statute name in the integrated search box, or go straight to a law by URL pattern law.go.kr/법령/<법령명>. On a law page, 조문 gives article-by-article text, 연혁 lists every past version with promulgation numbers, 신구법비교 shows an old/new redline, and 3단비교 stacks Act, Decree and Rule together.
sources.note: Sections labelled 영문법령 (English) are reference translations only and lag behind the Korean text.

sources.name: Korean Law Information Center (English)
sources.coverage: English renderings of current Acts and enforcement decrees, browsable by ministry and by legal field (constitutional, criminal, education, military affairs and others).
sources.desc: The government's own English front door to the statute database, useful when you know the English name of an Act but not the Korean one. It carries a searchable list of translated statutes with their enforcement dates.
sources.howto: Search by law title or full text in the English box, or browse the ministry and legal-field grids on the front page. Click through to the Korean version from any translated law to confirm the operative text.
sources.note: Each translated page carries the disclaimer that the text 'does not have any legal authority or official effect and may not reflect the most recent amendments'.

sources.name: Daehanmingug Yeongmun Beomnyeong
sources.en: Statutes of the Republic of Korea
sources.coverage: 3,033 current laws in English plus 20,480 former (superseded) versions, counted on the site's own front page; covers statutes, enforcement decrees, enforcement rules and other instruments.
sources.desc: The deepest English-language collection of Korean statutes, produced by the state legislation research institute and the source of most translations you see elsewhere, including on law.go.kr. It covers Acts, enforcement decrees, rules and administrative orders, with a Korean-English legal glossary.
sources.howto: Search by keyword, or filter by legal field, ministry, subject, promulgation date or enforcement date. Each entry shows the Korean title, promulgation number and the date the translation reflects, which is the number to check before relying on it.
sources.note: Marked official because KLRI is a state-funded research institute (the .re.kr domain is Korea's restricted namespace for research institutes, not a private .com) and is the body that produces the government's own English translations: the disclaimer on law.go.kr's English pages names it explicitly. Its copyright policy nonetheless states that KLRI material 'does not have legal or official authority' and 'shall be used only for reference'. Update lag behind the Korean text is common.

sources.name: Gukga Beomnyeong Jeongbo Gongdong Hwaryong
sources.coverage: Real-time feed of the same data as law.go.kr, exposed as roughly 191 separate APIs across 법령 (statutes, including historical versions and the English set), 행정규칙, 자치법규, 판례, 위원회 결정문, 법령해석례, 조약 and 별표·서식, each normally offered as a list query plus a full-text query.
sources.desc: The bulk and machine-readable route into Korean law. If you need the statute corpus programmatically rather than one page at a time, this is the official endpoint, split into list-query and full-text-query APIs.
sources.howto: Register for a key under OPEN API 신청, then consult 활용가이드 for per-dataset endpoints (law list, law full text, interpretations, ordinances). Sample source code and an error self-diagnosis tool are provided.
sources.note: Guides and parameter names are Korean-only. Ignore the dataset counts printed on the front page (5,100 laws, 25,000 government legislation records and so on): they are labelled 2013.10 개방 and are the holdings at the time each dataset was first opened, not current figures.

sources.name: Uian Jeongbo System
sources.authority: National Assembly of the Republic of Korea (대한민국 국회)
sources.coverage: Bills from the earliest National Assemblies through the current 22nd Assembly (제22대), which the site shows sitting in its 438th session; searchable by assembly number back through every prior Assembly.
sources.desc: Where a law comes from before it is a law: bill text, sponsors, committee review reports, floor votes by member, processing status including vetoes, plus petitions and budget documents.
sources.howto: Three search modes sit on the front page: 일반검색 matches bill titles word by word, 문서검색 searches inside proposal justifications, bill texts and committee review reports, and 지능형검색 is a vector search that takes a whole sentence and ranks related bills. Then filter by 제안기간, 의안종류, 제안자구분, 소관위원회 and 처리상태.
sources.note: Once a bill is promulgated, the operative text is the gazette version, not the bill page.

sources.name: Jonghap Beomnyul Jeongbo
sources.authority: Supreme Court of Korea (대법원) / National Court Administration
sources.coverage: Selected Supreme Court and lower-court judgments, court rules, statutes as applied by the courts, and legal literature references.
sources.desc: The judiciary's own case-law database, and the standard free route to Korean precedent in Korean. It offers directory browsing of 판례 by subject as well as citation and keyword search.
sources.howto: Reach it from the 종합법률정보 link on the Supreme Court front page, or go direct to the URL above. Search by case number in the Korean citation format (year + case-type letters + serial, e.g. 2016도4404), or browse the 판례 directory by field of law. Court rules and cited statutes are cross-linked from each judgment.
sources.note: The old address glaw.scourt.go.kr is dead: it returns NXDOMAIN from public resolvers while sibling scourt.go.kr hosts still resolve, so this is a retired subdomain rather than a geo-block. 종합법률정보 now lives inside portal.scourt.go.kr, which is where the Supreme Court's own site and the National Assembly Library both link it. law.go.kr's 판례 section (law.go.kr/precSc.do) carries an overlapping collection covering 대법원, 고등법원 and 지방법원 decisions and is the easier fallback.

sources.name: Sabeop Jeongbo Gonggae Portal
sources.coverage: Written judgments disclosed under the judgment-disclosure rules, judicial statistics and court information.
sources.desc: The channel for obtaining full written judgments of ordinary courts that are not in the selected-precedent database, including first-instance and appellate decisions, under the courts' disclosure scheme.
sources.howto: The portal splits the job across named services: 판결서 인터넷 열람 (the URL above) for searching and reading written judgments online, 판결서사본 제공신청 to request a copy, 판결서 방문열람 for in-person viewing, and 사법통계 for judicial statistics. Search by court, case number or keyword; judgments are delivered as redacted PDFs.
sources.note: Judgment retrieval requires identity verification and a per-judgment fee, and personal details are redacted. The same host also carries 종합법률정보 (the selected-precedent database) under a different menu, so check which of the two services you are actually in.

sources.name: Supreme Court of Korea - Decisions (English)
sources.coverage: A curated selection running from the 2000s to the present and actively maintained: the combined All list runs to roughly 184 pages and the newest entries at the time of checking were decided in May 2026. Chosen for international interest, not comprehensive.
sources.desc: The Supreme Court's own English translations of a curated set of judgments, grouped as Private Law, Administrative Law, Tax Law, Criminal Law and Intellectual Property Law. Each entry gives issues, holding, applicable statutes, cited cases and full reasoning.
sources.howto: Use the six category tabs, which map to URL parameters: mode=6 is All, mode=1 Private Law, mode=2 Administrative Law, mode=3 Tax Law, mode=4 Criminal Law, mode=5 IP Law. Lists are newest-first and paged via pageIndex. Each row gives the case number and decision date; opening it yields the full text, downloadable as an HTML file. Note that NewDecisionsView.work without parameters shows one fixed sample decision, not the list.
sources.note: The Court states that editorial additions such as 'main issues' and highlighted reasoning are not part of the original text; the Korean judgment governs.

sources.name: Heonbeop Jaepan Jeongbo Tonghap Geomsaek
sources.coverage: Constitutional Court decisions since the Court's establishment in 1988, plus Court publications and site content, in Korean with some English.
sources.desc: The Court's full decision database, covering constitutional review of statutes, constitutional complaints, competence disputes, impeachment and party dissolution. This is the authoritative place for the reasoning that strikes down or upholds a statute.
sources.howto: Results are split across five tabs: 통합검색, 한글판례, 영문판례, 발간자료 and 홈페이지. Enter a case number (e.g. 2016헌나1), a keyword, or a sentence of up to 100 characters for similarity search; the site's own syntax help gives quotation marks for an exact phrase, & or a space for AND, and | for OR. Then narrow with the detailed-search filters or re-search within results.

sources.name: Constitutional Court of Korea - Case Search (English)
sources.coverage: 694 decisions (the count shown on the search page), the most recent decided 18 December 2025, mostly as summaries with full text for cases of international significance.
sources.desc: English access to the Constitutional Court's docket, including the high-profile impeachment and party-dissolution decisions. Useful for identifying the case number to then look up in the Korean database.
sources.howto: Filter by keyword, case name, final decision (unconstitutional, constitutional, rejected, dismissed) or case type (Hun-Ka, Hun-Ma, Hun-Ba, Hun-Na, Hun-A), sort by case name, decision date or case number, and set 10 to 100 results per page. Search syntax is A+B or a space for AND and | for OR.
sources.note: Only the Korean versions are authoritative. The case-number filter is a trap: its year dropdown only offers 2010 to 2019, even though the collection contains later decisions such as 2021Hun-Ma946 (December 2025) and the 2024Hun-Na impeachment cases. Search those by keyword or case name instead, or use the Korean isearch.ccourt.go.kr.

sources.name: Jachi Beopgyu Jeongbo System
sources.en: Local Laws and Regulations Information System
sources.authority: Ministry of the Interior and Safety (행정안전부)
sources.coverage: Ordinances (조례) and rules (규칙) of all 17 metropolitan cities and provinces and all basic-level cities, counties and districts, plus local legislative notices.
sources.desc: The single national index of local legislation, which otherwise would have to be chased across hundreds of separate municipal sites. It also lets you compare how different local governments regulate the same subject.
sources.howto: Search by ordinance name or keyword and filter by local government; use the comparison search (비교 검색) to line up equivalent ordinances across jurisdictions, and 입법예고 for draft local rules out for comment.
sources.note: law.go.kr also carries 자치법규; ELIS is the fuller and more current index.

sources.name: Joyak Jeongbo System
sources.coverage: Bilateral and multilateral treaties to which Korea is a party, organised by country (국가별 조약 현황), by 34 subject areas including FTAs, and by year (연도별 통계), with signature and entry-into-force dates.
sources.desc: The authoritative register of Korea's treaty commitments, which matter domestically because a duly concluded and promulgated treaty has the same effect as an Act. Treaty texts and treaty numbers are published here alongside their gazette promulgation.
sources.howto: Use basic or advanced search, or browse via 분야별 조약 바로가기 (subject) and 국가별 조약 현황 (country); the 최근 발효조약 and 많이 본 조약 lists on the front page surface recent entries into force. Treaty titles are given in Korean with English alongside for international agreements.
sources.note: Interface is primarily Korean; the promulgated treaty text also appears in the Gwanbo with a treaty number.

sources.name: Tonghap Ipbeop Yego / Gungmin Chamyeo Ipbeop Center
sources.en: Integrated Legislative Notice / Public Participation Legislation Center
sources.coverage: Live and closed pre-announcement notices for national legislation, central-government administrative rules, and local government ordinances.
sources.desc: Where draft statutes, decrees and administrative rules are published for public comment before they exist as law. This is the earliest public sighting of a rule change and shows the drafting ministry and the comment deadline.
sources.howto: Pick the relevant tab, labelled on the live site as (부처)입법예고, (부처)행정예고 and (지방)입법예고, search by title or ministry, and open a notice for the draft text, the explanatory statement and the comment window. Registration (회원가입) and login are needed to file an opinion; reading is open.
sources.note: www.lawmaking.go.kr redirects here (verified). The site also runs 불편법령신고 for reporting burdensome regulations.

sources.name: Chatgi Swiun Saenghwal Beomnyeong Jeongbo
sources.coverage: Everyday legal topics reorganised by life situation, with core material available in 12 languages.
sources.desc: The government's plain-language layer over the statute book, arranged by situation (housing, employment, family, immigration) rather than by Act. Useful for identifying which Act governs a problem before going to law.go.kr for the operative text.
sources.howto: Browse the life-situation categories or search a topic in plain words; each explainer cites and links the underlying Acts and decrees on law.go.kr.
sources.note: Explanatory summaries only; the linked statute is the operative text.

sources.name: Gukhoe Beomnyul Doseogwan
sources.en: National Assembly Library - Legislative Information Portal
sources.coverage: Korean legislative background materials, committee and policy documents, constitutional materials, and the 외국법률번역DB with over 16,000 translated legal documents covering more than 170 countries and international organisations.
sources.desc: The research layer around Korean legislation: drafting history, committee papers, policy reports and comparative foreign-law translations that explain why a statute reads the way it does. Also the best Korean-language gateway to other countries' laws.
sources.howto: The top menus are 의회정보, 법률정보, 세계헌법정보, 발간자료, 의회지원서비스 and 안내. Foreign statutes sit under 법률정보 in 외국법률번역DB, 주요국 입법자료 and 세계법률가이드; foreign constitutions under 세계헌법정보 in 세계헌법DB. Filter by standing committee (국회운영, 법제사법, 정무 and the rest) or subject.
sources.note: Access downgraded from free-registration to free: the foreign-law and constitution databases open and display without logging in. A login is only needed for personalisation (My Library, mailing lists), and the licensed 학술DB / 신문DB collections remain restricted to on-site library terminals. Do not confuse this with 세계법제정보센터 (world.moleg.go.kr), which is a separate Ministry of Government Legislation site.

findLaw.task: Find the current consolidated text of an Act
findLaw.steps: Search the Act's Korean name in the integrated search box at the National Law Information Center, or go directly to law.go.kr/법령/<법령명>. Open the 조문 tab for the article-by-article text and check the header, which states the promulgation number and the enforcement date of the version you are reading.

findLaw.task: See what changed in a recent amendment, and read the text as promulgated
findLaw.steps: On the law's page at law.go.kr use 연혁 to list every past version and 신구법비교 for an old/new redline. For the authentic promulgated text, take the promulgation number and date from that page and pull the corresponding issue from the electronic gazette.

findLaw.task: Find a court decision interpreting a statute
findLaw.steps: For ordinary courts, search the Supreme Court's 종합법률정보 by case number in Korean citation form (year + case-type letters + serial) or browse the 판례 directory by field of law. Note that 종합법률정보 now sits inside portal.scourt.go.kr; the old glaw.scourt.go.kr address no longer resolves. law.go.kr's 판례 section (law.go.kr/precSc.do) covers Supreme Court, High Court and District Court decisions and is a good cross-check. Full written judgments not in the selected-precedent set come through 판결서 인터넷 열람 on the same portal.
findLaw.source: Comprehensive Legal Information (종합법률정보), Supreme Court of Korea

findLaw.task: Check whether a statute has been held unconstitutional
findLaw.steps: Search the Constitutional Court's integrated search by the Act's name or by case number (e.g. 2016헌바...), filtering by decision type such as 위헌 (unconstitutional) or 헌법불합치 (nonconforming). Cross-check the statute page on law.go.kr, which flags articles affected by a Constitutional Court ruling.

findLaw.task: Find subordinate legislation: enforcement decrees, ministerial rules and administrative notices
findLaw.steps: Open the parent Act on law.go.kr and use 3단비교, which stacks the Act, its Presidential Decree (시행령) and its Enforcement Rule (시행규칙) article by article. Ministry-level 훈령·예규·고시 sit under the separate 행정규칙 tab, searchable by issuing ministry.

findLaw.task: Find a local ordinance of a city, county or province
findLaw.steps: Search the ordinance name or subject at the Local Laws and Regulations Information System and filter by the local government concerned; the comparison search lines up equivalent ordinances across jurisdictions. Draft ordinances out for comment are under the local 입법예고 section.
findLaw.source: Local Laws and Regulations Information System (자치법규정보시스템)

findLaw.task: Read a Korean statute in English
findLaw.steps: Search the KLRI English statute database by title, ministry or subject, then check the promulgation number shown on the translation against the current Korean version on law.go.kr to see how far behind it is. The Ministry of Government Legislation's English portal at law.go.kr/eng carries the same translations with a ministry browse.
findLaw.source: Statutes of the Republic of Korea (대한민국 영문법령, KLRI)

subnational: Korea is a unitary state, but local autonomy is constitutionally guaranteed and there is a real body of subnational legislation. The 17 metropolitan cities and provinces and the basic-level cities, counties and autonomous districts enact ordinances (조례) through their local councils and rules (규칙) through their heads, all subordinate to national Acts and decrees. These are indexed nationally at the Local Laws and Regulations Information System (elis.go.kr), run by the Ministry of the Interior and Safety, with a mirror collection under 자치법규 on law.go.kr. Individual local governments also publish their own gazettes (시보/도보), which are the formal promulgation vehicle for their ordinances.
caveats: Only the Korean text is authentic. Every English version of a Korean statute, including the Constitution, is a reference translation: law.go.kr's English pages carry an explicit disclaimer that they have 'no legal authority or official effect and may not reflect the most recent amendments', KLRI says the same, and the Constitutional Court states that only the Korean versions are authoritative. The consolidated text on law.go.kr is the government's own working version and is reliable, but the legally promulgated text is the gazette version, and where an amendment has been promulgated but not yet taken effect the site will show both a current and a future-effective version, so check the enforcement date in the header. Case-law coverage is selective rather than complete: the Supreme Court's free database holds curated precedents, full written judgments of lower courts come through the disclosure portal with redactions and a fee, and the English decision sets from both apex courts are small curated samples. Court URLs also move without notice - 종합법률정보 has migrated off glaw.scourt.go.kr, which is now an unresolvable domain, into portal.scourt.go.kr, so older guides and citations pointing at glaw are all broken. Gazette metadata search is only complete from 25 March 2021 onward, and 1948-2000 issues are scanned images searched through a separate archive interface. Commercial Korean databases such as LawnB and free private aggregators are widely used in practice but are private publishers, not official sources.
